question:
Patient note:
A 34-year-old right-hand dominant male with no prior neurologic or psychiatric history was brought in by urban EMS ten minutes after a low-speed collision in which his electric scooter was clipped by the mirror of a passing delivery van; bystander video reviewed by paramedics showed him falling sideways, striking the left temporal region on asphalt while wearing only an unfastened half-shell helmet that dislodged on impact. Witnesses reported he never lost airway patency, uttered several incoherent phrases such as “where did the sidewalk go?” as he sat up, but then became increasingly agitated and attempted to walk into traffic before being guided to the curb. En route he received only a cervical collar, 4 L/min oxygen via simple facemask that he repeatedly tried to remove, and a finger-stick glucose of 109 mg/dL; no intravenous fluids, analgesics, sedatives, paralytics, or antiemetics were given. On arrival to the trauma bay he remains secured on a scoop stretcher, clothing dusty but free of blood. Initial vital signs prior to any emergency department intervention are blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg in the right brachial artery, pulse 104 beats per minute in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute with unlabored excursions, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing the same facemask, and tympanic temperature 36.8 °C. His eyelids are already parted as the team approaches, lashes blinking periodically without provocation, and the globes immediately shift to follow the overhead light as it swings across the ceiling grid; when a provider steps to the opposite side of the stretcher the patient turns his eyes and head to track the movement without any auditory cue. Pupils measure 3 mm bilaterally, are round, and contract briskly both directly and consensually. He speaks spontaneously in clear English, articulating full sentences, but his content is disordered: he states the current month is “Octember,” insists he is on his way to “catch the subway to Denver,” and, when asked the year, offers three different numbers in succession. He is unable to describe how the collision occurred, yet repeatedly asks whether the courier’s package was delivered. Despite the disorientation, his speech is fluent, grammatically intact, and of normal volume and prosody. Airway examination shows moist mucosa, uvula midline, no blood or dental injury, and an intact gag when a Yankauer tip gently touches the posterior pharynx; he coughs appropriately afterward. Breath sounds are vesicular and equal, percussion resonant, and chest wall inspection reveals only superficial road rash over the left anterior shoulder. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a regular tachycardic S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. He follows two-step commands reliably: when asked to close his eyes and then stick out his tongue, he complies promptly; on request to grip the examiner’s fingers he produces symmetric 5/5 handgrip and releases on instruction; he lifts each leg off the board for five seconds when told, despite complaining of left hip soreness. Cranial nerve screening reveals symmetric facial movement, full extra-ocular range, and shoulder shrug strong against resistance. No drift is seen on pronator testing. There is a 5 × 3 cm boggy hematoma with mild oozing over the left temporoparietal scalp; no palpable skull step-off. Palpation along the cervical spinous processes elicits tenderness at C3–C4 but no crepitus. Sensory exam to light touch and pinprick is intact in all dermatomes, though the patient intermittently withdraws saying “that tickles” regardless of stimulus location. Coordination is preserved with accurate finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin when attempted. Deep tendon reflexes are 2 + and symmetric in biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles; plantar responses are downgoing. Tone remains normal without spasticity or flaccidity. No abnormal posturing, tremor, or myoclonus is observed. Based on the observed spontaneous eye opening, confused yet articulated speech, and consistent obedience to commands, his overall Glasgow Coma Scale score is calculated at 14 out of 15. Lungs are clear, abdomen soft and non-tender with active bowel sounds, and pelvis stable to compression. Long bones are aligned without deformity; there is superficial abrasion over the left lateral thigh but no step-off. Skin is warm, capillary refill under two seconds. Bedside point-of-care hemoglobin reads 14.2 g/dL; rapid serum ethanol sent by venous sample is pending. Two 18-gauge peripheral IV catheters have been placed but remain heparin-locked, and no medications or intravenous fluids have yet entered his system since crossing the ambulance threshold, ensuring the neurologic findings described represent his untreated baseline. Portable anterior-posterior chest radiograph obtained on the stretcher shows clear lung fields and an intact clavicular girdle, while a non-contrast head CT and CT cervical spine are ordered STAT but not yet performed. Neurosurgery, trauma surgery, and radiology have been consulted; serial neurochecks are scheduled every fifteen minutes. Throughout observation to this point he keeps his eyes open of his own accord, speaks with persistent though misplaced confidence about imaginary destinations, and promptly follows every motor instruction provided, all prior to any sedative, analgesic, or antihypertensive therapy.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow Coma Scale sums the best eye, verbal, and motor responses at admission.
- Eyes: Already open and tracking movement without prompting → spontaneous opening, E4.
- Verbal: Speaks in sentences and answers questions, but is disoriented → confused conversation, V4.
- Motor: Reliably follows commands to grip and release → obeys commands, M6.
Total = 4 + 4 + 6 = 14 of 15.
Final answer: 14
